newsitem.title: USA: Republicans, Democrats meet in congressional debate.
newsitem.headline: Republicans, Democrats meet in congressional debate.

text.p: Republican and Democratic congressional leaders square off Sunday in a nationally televised debate that will kick off an intense autumn battle for control of the House and Senate.
The matchup will pit two radically different visions of what government should be as each party seeks to present a new face to voters.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich says he wants to showcase his party's vision of less government and more individual freedom.

But Gingrich has another agenda in the debate, which is to try to show voters he is not the radical he has been branded. Stung by ethics charges, Gingrich is trying to resuscitate his image, and by extension, that of his House colleagues.

"My guess is the American people are going to look at this and feel pretty darn good that the 104th Congress ended ... ahead of schedule, under budget and in a cooperative manner," Gingrich told reporters Saturday.

In defence of the Georgia Republican,, House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston, R-Louisiana, told reporters, "The American people should see the side I have seen of him over the last two years. He is extraordinarily capable."

Public Television is sponsoring the debate, which will be televised live from Williamsburg, Va.'s historic House of Burgesses, the restored 18th century home of the first legislature to meet in the Western hemisphere.

The existence of this debate, the first nationally televised forum of this type for legislative leaders, is owed largely to the increased prominence of Congress in national politics since Gingrich brought his brand of political revolution to Washington.

Gingrich will be accompanied by Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, who brought a new tone of conciliation to the Senate when he ascended to the top spot after Bob Dole chose to seek the presidency full-time.

On the other side, Democrats want to present a new "Team Democrat" to voters, saying they have learned from the 1994 congressional losses that Americans did not like their liberal agenda and that they, too, have moved to the middle.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota and House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri plan to present their case for a "Families First" agenda which stresses government's role in providing a safety net for children and parents.

"We are going to try to lay out what the Democratic party is all about. What we see as our vision for the next two years -- how important it is to connect with working families," Daschle told reporters this week.
As Republicans strive to display their ability to govern, Democrats will strive all the more to paint the Republican party as extremist.

"It's an election year conversion, but the citizens are not going to give them absolution," Democrat Patrick Leahy of Vermont said after Republicans agreed Saturday to a budget that restored much of the president's spending for education and domestic programmes.

If Republicans retain the majority after the Nov. 5 elections, it will be the first time they have held control of the House for more than one term since the 1929 election ended a 14-year Republican reign.
